utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I do understand that there is a preliminary matter you would like to raise, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Yeah, regarding that document with the handwriting on it on the back, P2097, we have an original and if you'd like to look at it it's -- I've got it here now in the binder. The only glitch that we noticed that you recall I made reference to a stamp from the 65th Protection Regiment, that was in the English translation. We cannot find it - Mr. Ivetic and I both looked at this this morning and could not find that and based on the ERN range it should be there if it existed. So we may need to send this back for revision to remove that unless there's something else that would explain what that is there for. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has looked at it. I did understand that you, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Ivetic, have looked at it together as well. Could I ask whether the objection on the basis of authenticity stands or -- because that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that I objected to the document, Your Honour. Your Honours had asked about the handwriting whether it was on the back of one of the originals or whether it was a separate piece that had been added to the document. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was my recollection there was an issue about authenticity as well because it was of the Pecanac --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the next one which I'm about to get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This one then -- we have MFI'd this one, not -- it's in evidence. We have seen it now. It's clear now where the handwriting comes from. Yes, it was admitted and I only then put that question about the handwriting. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the next one that you've just referred to, the May 28th intel report on Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica from the Pecanac collection, as I had recalled yesterday, it did become evidence in the Tolimir case. It was tendered through Colonel Petar Salapura, the chief of intelligence of the Main Staff. And, as you recall, he testified 92 ter here and in our zeal we did not put that part of the transcript in his 92 ter package. So that part where he speaks of this and the document didn't come in through him this time, but it did come in through him. He spoke of it briefly in Tolimir. And if I may go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I briefly address another matter, that is, D353 was first MFI'd, one of the reasons being that there was no translation -- or at that moment perhaps the reason to be that there was no translation. Then the translation was uploaded but when, I think yesterday, I admitted D353 into evidence, I overlooked that there was another issue, it was a document which was prepared by the Defence and it had got something to do with the entries in a log, I think it was, and there were objections on the basis of the content of the document as well. So we'd like to further hear the response of -- first of all, the -- now the translation is there, to hear from the Prosecution exactly what the issue is and then from the Defence a response to those objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not necessarily to be done immediately but soon I would say. Good morning, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and awaiting that debate, D353 returns now and is MFI'd again and we'll decide later on admission. Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. McCloskey will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'd like to go back briefly to the May 28th intel report from Pecanac, it's 65 ter 25996, and I -- as you've stated, you've had a chance to go through that. Can you tell us how impressed or unimpressed you were with the intelligence in this -- in this document? In particular, can you tell us in your opinion what kind of sources would have been used to gather this sort of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- I'm impressed, again as one intelligence professional to another, in this case because it is clear that the intelligence organs of the Army of the Republika Srpska did dedicate a significant amount of time and effort to trying to gain as much clarity about the composition of all of the forces in the three enclaves that existed there, to include the forces of the ABiH as well as the composition of the UN forces there performing their functions. I gather from both this document as well as my knowledge of other practices by the VRS intelligence service at various levels, many of these they would have gotten from physical observations by command posts or at forward observation posts. They did actively collect information from the various translators or individuals who were working for the UN to try to get information. They -- as well as the ABiH, where possible, they tried to intercept radio communications of the opposing enemy forces in order to glean information from that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on in the narrative as we approach the Srebrenica operation, and I would like us to go to a document the Court has seen, P1153. This is an order from the Drina Corps command, General Zivanovic. As we can see from the first page entitled: "Taking physical control of the Zeleni Jadar facilities and asphalt road," 2 June. Can you briefly explain to us the -- any military importance you have for this particular area. I think you've mentioned it briefly before. And then I'll ask you one or two questions about this document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I discussed yesterday, because of where the VRS forces were arrayed outside of the enclave in May, they recognised that before they could launch any operations towards the enclave, they would have to undertake some preparatory operations in order to clear a particular area in order to extend the road network into the enclave to support their own forces in the future. This particular document is an order from the Drina Corps to elements of the Bratunac Brigade as well as elements of the Zvornik Brigade that would participate in that type of a limited operation designed essentially to clear a road area and also as a consequence to essentially remove one UN check-point from its present location in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we -- as we look at this document we could go to number -- page 2 in the English and then probably page 2 in the B/C/S just to get a review of it. We see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- before we do so, could we go back to page 1. I see that it comes from the Drina Corps command forward command post. It says: "Order," and apart from the Bratunac Brigade command it's also addressed to the commander of the Drina Corps, which -- is that really what it -- or do we -- should we read that as to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade manoeuvre battalion of the Drina Corps? It's -- I'm a bit surprised to see an order given by a forward command post of the Drina Corps command to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is an issue that's come up before and I'm sure Mr. Butler can address it, I believe, as he has before in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could just say that in the B/C/S there is not a separate recipient identified as the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wondered whether "komandantu manevarskog bataljona DK" whether that stands for something different as we find in the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're correct, sir. It appears to be a bit of a mistranslation. Obviously it is the corps commander who is at the IKM who is writing this document and it's addressed to the Bratunac Brigade command and the Bratunac Brigade manoeuvre battalion of the DK, which, if you read into the article or the order, it's clearly the Drina Wolves unit of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, perhaps it would be better to have a corrected translation uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Butler, have you seen sometimes high-ranking officers sending documents to themselves or to their offices sometimes when they're away from their normal headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is a pattern. There will be documents that we look at down the line, for example, where an officer of the Main Staff who happens to be at the Drina Corps headquarters on a certain day will send an order out and will also make sure that a copy of that order goes back to his headquarters for his staff, not only for them to see but also so that he has a record of the actual order that he published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But that's a different situation compared to this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. I think we were at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see from reeding this that General Zivanovic has given particular directions on how to approach the UNPROFOR soldiers and OPs, including, as we see on that first paragraph up in the English, well, actually the third paragraph in that first cluster as, talks about firing warning shots and then if they failed to follow the order one should fire a Zolja hand-held rocket-launcher into the power generator. It goes on to say in the next paragraph, under 2, the same thing, basically, when they don't surrender, neutralise -- it says: "Use a Zolja to neutralise the personnel carrier ..." And I would just call your attention to that because they have a reference in another document that I would -- that we'll get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I would offer this into -- I'm sorry, it's already into evidence. So could we go now to the next document, 65 ter 19557.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This again is from the Drina Corps command, the Pribicevac IKM, it's the next day, the 3rd of June, this is a regular combat report in the name of Major Milenko Jevdjevic. Do you recall who Jevdjevic is -- was back then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Jevdjevic was the, I believe, a -- the commander of the communications unit of the Drina Corps back in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we see this is to the Main Staff and under the "enemy" section: "After a successful operation and forceful expulsion of UNPROFOR from the Zeleni Jadar post ..." And then it goes on to talk about the enemy. In your view, what -- does this have anything to do with the previous operation that we saw and just discussed the -- Zivanovic's order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is connected. This is the report from the Drina Corps back to the higher headquarters, advising them of the results of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in your view, this -- would General Mladic -- should he have been aware of this information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He should have been made aware of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we look at the bottom of the first page in English, under "our forces," it says: "In a very precise and professional operation," then they're not exactly sure what's said but it appears to be VRS forces "forced the UNPROFOR check-point in Zeleni Jadar to withdraw in panic to Srebrenica ..." And: "They were stopped on the road in the sector of an elevation ..." And then it notes that: "Force was used but there were no injuries to the UN personnel." And if we go to the next page in English, it's under paragraph 3 so we need to go on to the next page in B/C/S. We note there that it states that: "We have had no casualties. We have expended small amounts of ammunition and three Zoljas." Is this consistent with the order that Zivanovic gave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's consistent in so much as his direction to use those under certain circumstances. It would appear that at least three of them were expended; again, however, I have not read the Dutch version of this particular operation so I can't comment as to whether or not they were used precisely as Colonel or General Zivanovic intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I bring this up to ask you, do we see anything in the attack on the enclave itself that -- any attacks on the UN OPs by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When the Krivaja 95 operation begins, one of the patterns that one sees with the advancing VRS forces as they come up to these UN check-points is that they are operating under a great deal of restraint. They do not want to engage the UN forces in combat operations, yet they know that they need to get around those particular check-points or otherwise bypass them. So there is a great deal of manoeuvre and fire that's in the general direction of but not at the UNPROFOR and those check-points in order to coerce them to leave the positions under threat but not to actually attack them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, I'd offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 19557 will be Exhibit P2100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go to P1087, that's the map book. It should be page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a map I think the Trial Chamber is familiar with. It's a map of the enclave from the VRS where General Mladic has signed it up in the left-hand corner, saying "I approve." And it's entitled "Krivaja 95." And we'll see from this page some of the other translations. But, Mr. Butler, there is -- I think we'll acknowledge the date on -- the only date we see here is 12 July where it's a handwritten note noted that: "Completed - this was Serbian and it's now Serbian, 12 July," signed by General Mladic, but there is no other -- other date on this approval document. When, in your view, would a map like this be approved in relation to an operation such as this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using the command and staff manual of the Yugoslav national army, which the VRS did as part of their command and staff processes during the war, it lays out in great detail the military staff process and the deliberative planning process. Normally for complex operations, the military practice is that the headquarters that was planning the operation - in this particular case the Drina Corps - would brief their higher headquarters and obtain the approval of the higher commander before the operation was finalised and the orders were given out. Very often, in order for everyone to be able to completely visualise all aspects of the plan, this briefing would be given using the aid of a map graphic, such as you see here. My examination of this document reflects that it is the map graphic that would correspond to what is the Krivaja 1995 plan. On the lower right-hand corner, you have the signature of the corps commander at the time, General Zivanovic, where he submits this plan. And as per the military practice that the VRS undertook, on the upper left-hand corner you have the approval of the superior commander, in this case General Mladic. I understand from prior testimony in a prior case, the origin of the writing on this particular map dated 12 July 1995, but it is my opinion that this actual map graphic minus that writing on 12 July was actually produced as part of the Drina Corps's presentation of the Krivaja 95 plan to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us -- we will see the plan itself, but can you give us any kind of a date range or estimate regarding when you think that would have been based on what -- your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the plan itself was put on paper on 2 July, so I believe that the plan was actually briefed to the Main Staff shortly before 2 July 1995. I think between late May and the first day of -- or, I'm sorry, late June/first day of July, 1995. I believe that some individuals associated with that have testified in previous cases - they may have testified in this Trial Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we first move the map up a bit so that we can see the lower right-hand side part of it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now can we go to 65 ter 5691.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're getting to that, Mr. Butler, this will be a Main Staff report to the president of the Republika Srpska dated 2 July, where the -- it's basically the Main Staff version of the daily combat reports which the Court has heard about to the various corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in both languages where we have the Drina Corps section --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we -- you deal with that document, Mr. McCloskey, I see in your list of documents to be used that the map we just looked at, P1087, is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't remember why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe that was the map book that was part of the admin hearing that we had -- we had attempted to clear up at the admin hearing that we both -- though, you may be actually ruling on that still. Perhaps Mr. Ivetic recalls. I think that the ball may be in your court on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, this particular map was not one of the ones that was objected to. The ones that were objected to were in the A series of the map book at the beginning that were generated by the Office of the Prosecutor based upon unknown information, and I believe we are still awaiting a final decision on that. But this map that was used, this particular page, I don't believe was subject to that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That refreshes my recollection as well, yes. We'll pay attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President? I just missed your last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that it refreshes my recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and we'll pay attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. So we're now at this Main Staff report for 2 July. It should be at page 3, yes. And under the "Drina Corps - situation in the corps," it says that: "The corps units are in full combat readiness and are keeping a strong hold on positions reached." And then this is the part I want to ask you: "Unengaged forces are being prepared for the forthcoming active combat operations." What in your view, if you have one, what operations are they talking about there? They're not -- they don't tell us outwardly. They don't tell the president outwardly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Given the date of this document and the context of what's being discussed, they're talking about the Krivaja 95 operation, which as part of the operation required units to disengage some forces from their current positions and to move them towards the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in this -- if we look at the -- we don't need to but we'll see the last page of this, this is under General Miletic and -- standing in for Milovanovic who is at the Krajina. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 05691 will be Exhibit P2101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2101 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P1465.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document the Trial Chamber has seen. It is the -- from the command of the Drina Corps in the name of General Zivanovic dated 2 July entitled "Krivaja 95." And this is the attack order that you've been referring to, is it not, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go over some bits of this. The first part we see is largely a discussion of the layout of the Muslim forces, though we do see in paragraph 1 a reference to an order to cut the Drina Corps area of responsibility in two, something I think we'll all recall hearing before. Now let's go to page 3 in the English, it should be B/C/S page 2, I want to take you to what's numbered 2. And it says: "The Command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to Operations Directive number 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff, and on the basis of the situation in the Corps area of responsibility, has tasks of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone, as soon as possible, in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and to reduce them to their urban areas." Now, first of all, can you tie-in this reference to 7 and 7/1 to your opinion regarding whether 7/1 had replaced directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I testified yesterday, it is my view that directive 7/1 supplemented directive 7 and it did not replace directive 7. The fact that in this particular order they reference both documents and not the most recent document, directive 7/1, again, it's one of these -- it's this type of reference that I use to support my opinion that directive 7 did -- was supplemented and not -- or basically superseded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then to that last part, the mention of splitting apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, you've mentioned that before. Is that the same analysis from your -- the previous references, or because of this document is there any change in what you have said about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I believe the guidance remains consistent with directive 7 and 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've already talked about what that meant. And this last reference, "... and to reduce them to their urban areas." First of all, what does that mean to you? We saw from the -- Pecanac's report that the enclave was roughly, I think, 150 square kilometres, we've seen the map ourselves. So what's the urban area in size, roughly, as far as you know, to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge is it's approximately 1 kilometre by 3 kilometres. So you're talking a very small area in the valley focused around the immediate town of Srebrenica and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what do you believe this means, this reference to "reduce the enclave"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says. By reducing the enclave to that very small urban area, at least militarily, it would be impossible for the 28th Infantry Division to remain, to hide in the enclave, or to conduct any military-related activities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What would you expect the civilian population to do upon the attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- what I would expect is that, you know, given the background and history of the area, the civilian population would flee towards Srebrenica. They would not seek to remain where they were and, essentially, find themselves in Bosnian Serb military-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if the bulk of the population of the Srebrenica enclave fled into the urban area of Srebrenica, what kind of situation would that create?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it would create a situation analogous to that which existed in late March/early April of 1993, where you had a rather large civilian population essentially jammed into a small area that did not have the ability to support that population and where you had, in essence, you know, as that crisis wore on the United Nations forces were moving thousands of civilians from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you referring to the time-period when General Morillon stepped in, and we can see him on film amongst the crowd of Srebrenica, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go down to paragraph -- the bottom of paragraph 4, where it's under "objective." It says: "By a surprise attack, to separate and reduce the size of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, to improve the tactical position of the forces in depth of the area, and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." What does this mean, in your view, "create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is consistent with the language of directive 7. There was no intention, at least as far as the mili diary documents reflect, that the VRS, even in the abstract event that the 28th Division could somehow be militarily defeated, that they would still want the enclave or a UN protected zone to exist there, even if it simply consisted of civilians under UN protection. Their objective, as articulated in many documents, was the elimination of the enclave, not simply the elimination of the military threat of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this an order for an all-out attack on the enclave to take them or something else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And that is the unique thing about both directive 7 and this order. They did not order an attack to capture the town of Srebrenica, effectively eliminating the enclave. They did not believe that they could -- at least in the initial phase, it was clear that they didn't believe that they could obtain that objective, particularly, you know -- it was a prudent decision obviously in light of the perceived strength of the 28th Division, the relative limited number of their own friendly forces that could attack, as well as the unpredictable nature, particularly after June of 1995, where NATO had actually bombed VRS forces, the unpredictable nature and response that they may get out of the UN or NATO. So they didn't believe at the early stages of this operation that they could capture the town and they did not plan to. They did, however, believe that they could launch offensive operations and be successful to a point, which would then lead to a further set of circumstances, again perhaps in the same vein as 1993, where the United Nations themselves would choose to end the presence of the enclaves and have the UN evacuate the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek some clarification of one of your previous answers. You said: "Their objective, as articulated in many documents, was the elimination of the enclave, not simply the elimination of the military threat of the 28th Division." But the line before that you said that: "... that they would still want the enclave or the UN protected zone to exist there." Now, eliminating the enclave and still wishing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's -- I don't believe I said that, I hope I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- therefore, I'm seeking clarification. Perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To repeat, as envisioned in the military documents that I've discussed, the VRS military leadership had always put in those documents the elimination of the enclave. It is not a circumstance - at least as far as I can tell from the documents - that the VRS ever would envision a situation where the 28th Division was militarily defeated and no longer a factor, yet there would still be a UN protected enclave deep within the territory of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go now right to July 9th, after some days of combat, and to D288. This is a document from the Drina Corps forward command post at Pribicevac dated 9 July from the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, General Krstic. And it describes the -- some of the combat and the areas. And then in paragraph 3 entitled: "Decision for further operations," he states: "Taking advantage of the success achieved, regroup the forces and carry out a vigorous and decisive attack towards Srebrenica." And then as we go down to paragraph 4, it talks a bit about the UNPROFOR check-points, and concludes that paragraph with: "UNPROFOR forces from the base in Potocari village did not intervene at the check-points or attack our forces." Does General Krstic's interim combat report to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps command, does that change the nature of this -- this objective at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the success of the combat operations, as envisioned or as articulated in this interim report, General Krstic is advising his superiors that they're going to continue combat operations towards the town, not necessarily to capture the town. But he's certainly at this juncture raising the prospect that that option may for the very first time for the VRS be available. And as other documents that happened in the future demonstrate, that then led to a decision predicated obviously by discussions, where the objective of Krivaja 95 is then changed by the president of the Republika Srpska to include the capture or the liberation of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Taking us briefly back to directive 7, where you'll recall there's a reference after making life unbearable to starting a plan should UNPROFOR leave the enclave, and then we see down here, as I just read, that during these combat days Krstic is telling his command that the UNPROFOR did not intervene in the check-points or attack the forces. Would this have been -- the UNPROFOR's activity been a factor in the VRS command and decision to go forward and change the objective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that with respect to what General Krstic thought it was as well as the lack of any activity by NATO at the same time. The perception, of course, that he had was that the UN was not going to defend the enclave based on the activities of the UNPROFOR to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to P1466, a document that the Trial Chamber has seen, I believe, several times. And it is dated 9 July, very urgent, to the president of the Republika Srpska, for information at Drina Corps IKM, Generals Gvero and Krstic personally, and it's in the name of Zdravko Tolimir and notes, among other things, that: "The President of Republika Srpska has been informed of the successful combat operations around Srebrenica ..." and the results achieved. And then it says: "The President of the Republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of the Muslim terrorist gangs and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." It goes on to say: Take care of the civilian population and follow the Geneva Conventions, as we can see there. What is your -- first of all, does this provide us an indication of the whereabouts of any senior officers? We see this is in the name from General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this date -- I mean, one of the first things that's notable is that General Gvero, a Main Staff officer, is present with General Krstic at the Drina Corps forward command post, observing the operations. As I testified yesterday, based off of the documents and how the Main Staff operated, it was a relatively common practice for an officer of the Main Staff to be at a subordinate formation during a significant event like this, to be able to monitor the operations and, as necessary, provide guidance from the Main Staff. General Tolimir in this particular context, I believe he's at the Main Staff headquarters at Han Pijesak on 9 July 1995 and that this particular -- he was the one who drafted this based off of the results of a meeting with the president of the republic. I don't know where that meeting took place or who participated in that meeting, where the president was briefed on the results of the operation to date and presumably briefed by the military that the objective could now be changed to include the taking of Srebrenica and offering that up for the approval of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you say that the objective could be changed. What does this document do in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is the manifestation of the order to change the objective by the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this language, "the president of the republic is satisfied with the results of the combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation ..." what does the term "has agreed" -- what meaning can you give to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, what this supposes in this context is that the military officials who briefed General Karadzic [sic] of this plan obviously briefed him on the military situation, briefed him on their capabilities, but -- and made recommendations to the president of the republic as the supreme commander of the armed forces. That -- as one looks at the structure of the Republika Srpska Supreme Command body, again it bears noting that while officers like General Mladic and General Milovanovic advised that -- the Supreme Command and can make proposals to it, they are not actually members of the Supreme Command; it is a strictly civilian body. So in this particular context, it's the role of the military to make proposals and ultimately the role of the Commander-in-Chief of the Supreme Command - in this case the president of the republic - to accept those proposals and make them as orders or to modify those proposals and then they're transmitted back down through those officers for implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question. You said the Supreme Command was a strictly civilian body. Was there an army officer on that civil -- on the Supreme Command, a minister of defence, or am I wrong on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of defence -- there was not a VRS officer on it. The Supreme Command consisted of both the minister of defence and the minister of the interior, but there was not a member of the VRS Main Staff who was a member of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the minister of defence, was that person a military man, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall who the minister of defence was in 1995. I think it was still Subotic who was nominally a colonel, but played more of a role of a civilian than a military officer at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we do so, could I ask one question, just whether I understood your testimony well. Was the plan always to reduce the size of the enclave and in the long term for it to be eliminated but not initially by taking over the town of Srebrenica itself? And that only in this respect on the 9th of July plans were changed and that the elimination on the long term changed more or less by taking over the town? Is that how I have to understand the main line of what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, looking at the Krivaja 95 order, there is no mention of an objective being the capture or liberation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- the base plan was successfully executed and only on the 9th of July, based on the success of the base plan was an initial -- was a further objective then given to now, for the first time, actually physically capture or liberate the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which also would result in the immediate termination of the existence of the enclave as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it was not reduced anymore, it wouldn't exist any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We take a break. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to correct myself. I said a few things this morning about D353 and I referred to it as a chart where there were objections. Now, it -- what I said is actually related to D354, which is MFI'd, which is a table that the Defence used during the cross-examination of Witness Turkusic. Yesterday through an informal communication, the Defence informed the Prosecution and the Chamber that the translation for D354, MFI, had been uploaded into e-court and asked for admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In an e-mail sent later yesterday, the Prosecution objected to the admission of the document and the Chamber invites the parties to put their submissions regarding D354, MFI, on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I know when you said it's 354, we will propose to maintain this document MFI'd until our ballistics experts are here. So actually we are not asking for this document to be admitted yet only to -- that translation to be attached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to attach it and we will wait and see and D354 keeps the status of being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we were so impolite as to deal with other matters when you entered the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey will, however, correct this and continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We now on July 10 -- excuse me, July 9. We have the object changing and can you tell us were any special police and MUP forces brought in to the Srebrenica operation after that decision to now actually take the town itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In light of the decision to take the town itself, an acknowledgement that additional forces would be required to do that, orders were given by the Ministry of the Interior to have a number of special police units sent to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us who was to be in command of that -- those units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of those particular units from the special police forces, primarily from Jahorina, was Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber has heard a bit about him, seen him on the video with his forces around Sandici and in Kravica. And can you tell us -- and we'll get into some documents, but can you just briefly tell us in your view when Borovcanin and his forces arrived to the battle area, whose -- under whose command were they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the Republika Srpska Law on the Ministry of the Interior under a state of imminent threat of war or under a state of war, when military -- when police forces are operating in a military zone, they do fall under the command of the military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall, are there some basic requirements of people who have to make requests and approve these things?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Many of the provisions under which the police will serve under military command and control are outlined in this particular law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 4048. And we can see that this is from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior, cabinet of the minister. It's dated 10 July. It comes out under the name of -- we have it Staff Commander Tomislav Kovac. Do you recall his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, in July of 1995 at this time he was the acting minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see that it's to the commander of the Special Police Brigade and various staffs of those forces, Trnovo, Vogosca, Bijeljina, and then the Zvornik CJB and the Sarajevo CJB and the Jahorina police training camp. Now, is this group a mixture of special police forces and regular CJB, which are basically civilian police forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the first line we see underneath those folks is: "Pursuant to the order of the Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska Armed Forces, and in order to crush the enemy offensive being carried out from the safe area of Srebrenica." We see that that would be Radovan Karadzic of course. And is this -- is his approval required under the law, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we see the order, I won't read it all, but it's: "Detach a part of RS MUP that are taking part in the combat operations on the Sarajevo front and send them ... on the 11th ... to the Srebrenica sector." And it lists the group of units, Special Police Detachment Sekovici, 1st Company of PJP. Without getting into the translation, are PJP, are those civilian police officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We generally -- when we look at the acronym "PJP," we generally associate that with the municipal police forces or, as Mr. McCloskey says, the civilian police forces as separate from the special police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know the Defence will agree, as they have many times, that the translation of those units "special police unit" causes confusion. So we just will stick with the "PJP" as opposed to the translation. It also says: "... a mixed company of the joint RSK, Serbian and RS MUP forces and a company from the training camp at Jahorina." Then it designates Borovcanin, the deputy commander of the special police, as the commander of these MUP units. And then it basically describes how he's supposed to leave the Trnovo battle-field with the destination of the area to report to General Krstic. Now -- to the Bratunac area. As far as you know, were there any Serbian MUP units working with Borovcanin at the Sarajevo-Trnovo front?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm aware that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's -- I want to come back to this important document, but let's for now jump to 65 ter 40 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I would like to ask a question in relation to item 5 of this order. Mr. McCloskey has used the term "to report to General Krstic." In the English translation it is -- there is another term "to make contact with the Corps Chief of Staff, General Krstic." What is your understanding of the word "to make contact," if that is the right translation, bearing in mind that Mr. Borovcanin had a certain rank, I don't know exactly, he was deputy commander of the Special Police Brigade and to make contact with the general of the army. What is your understanding what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, going -- going to this particular paragraph, at the time General Krstic is the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and he's also known to be the actual commander of the forces involved in Krivaja 1995. So he is the senior military person on the ground at the time this order is written as far as the Ministry of the Interior people know. So it would be normal for them to order Borovcanin to report to or to make contact with the senior military officer so he can receive the instructions as to what his units were supposed to do or how they were supposed to integrate themselves into the conflict. As it turns out and I believe as Mr. Borovcanin notes, by the time he gets there and makes contact, in fact now General Mladic is there. So as -- by custom, Borovcanin's going to report to the senior officer, which is General Mladic, and receive his orders from that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I will get back and we'll get a little more detail on that, but -- and if we could skip ahead and I move to 65 ter 4078. And this is a document in the name of -- that Borovcanin has done entitled -- well, from the MUP, Special Police Brigade Trnovo. And we see that it's talking -- it's dated 1 July and it's talking about various combat activities on the -- at the Trnovo front. And it also makes a note, we see on the third line of the English: "... and two platoons from each of the Kajman, Plavi and Skorpija detachments (the MUP of Serbia) have been attacking the Lucevik feature ..." This Skorpija MUP unit, are they the now-well-known unit involved in the video of executions in the Trnovo area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe this is the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so -- so what's -- what's going on here with the special police and these MUP units? They appear to be in combat together?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One of -- things that it was customarily seen through the conflict is that in some battle-field areas Serbian MUP units were rotated into Bosnia and Herzegovina to fight alongside the Republika Srpska MUP forces for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04078 will be Exhibit P2102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2102 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go back to 65 ter 4048, and as I'd noted earlier we saw that there was a reference that Serbian MUP would be coming along with Borovcanin. Has the investigation or have any of your documents revealed any information on whether or not the Serbian MUP actually came to the Srebrenica-Bratunac-Konjevic Polje battle area during the time-frame here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It was an area that both I looked at with respect to the military documents and the investigation pursued, and I'm not aware of any information that, you know, notwithstanding this order that they accompany the forces, that they actually in fact did accompany those forces and were in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And getting back to paragraph 5, where we have that Borovcanin: "On arrival at his destination the unit commander is obliged to make contact with the Corps Chief of Staff, General Krstic." And you've referenced this regarding Judge Fluegge's question, but can you tell us do you -- what is your interpretation of now any command relationship between Borovcanin and Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context and in accordance with the RS law on the issue, once Borovcanin makes contact or reports to the senior army commander, he falls under that individual's command as well as the police units there for the duration of the assigned mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04048 will be Exhibit P2103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2103 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'd like to take us to a document. You do have it cited in your report, 65 ter 4387. It is from the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska and is a law, and I would like us to go to page 12 in the English. It should be in the Serbian page 4 and 5. And it's entitled: "The use of police units in combat operations." And I think after reading the bottom of the page there in the Serbian, we can now go to the next page in the Serbian. But, Mr. Butler, looking here at these Articles 13, especially Articles 14, where they're talking about the requirements of the command when there's joint combat operations, is this the law you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you clarify this to us, does -- what does Borovcanin retain in terms of command when he is -- once he is under the command of the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- particularly as listed in Article 14, once police forces fall under command of the army, the army's control over them is not absolute. For example, Borovcanin has been appointed as the commander of that police unit. It is not under the army's authority to relieve Colonel Borovcanin and then appoint him with somebody else. The army cannot, for example, disband a police unit and then use the individual soldiers of that unit to plus-up army units. So there are limits to what the army can do with police units, and in most situations need limits to the extent that the army can use police forces are known in advance to the military and to the police commanders so there's no confusion in the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04387 will be Exhibit P2104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we looked at a certain page, I think you showed that, where the resubordination and the structure of police forces in combat are dealt with. I see the totality of the document is 44 pages. Now, do we need all of that in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My view, Mr. President, would be no, that the first page and the two pages of the Serbian would be fine and the one page of English would be fine as far as we're concerned. We normally don't pick out the law like that, but I think it's -- I would fully agree that we should simplify this and I have no problem with doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the Defence, is there any need for further context, because what we looked at is specifically and I think exclusively the command structure over police forces which are used for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would like to defer until the end of cross-examination as to the -- as to whether certain other articles might be referred to or not, but I would agree with opposing counsel, that there's no need for the entire -- the entire 65 ter number to be -- that is in e-court to be admitted. It's just the ones that would be used by the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for the time being, Exhibit P2104 as uploaded in e-court is marked for identification. The parties are invited to agree on what are the relevant pages we should look at, apart, of course, from the first page which gives the necessary details of the Official Gazette in which it was published. Yes, it is a photocopy of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, on -- continuing on this related issue and getting a bit off our narrative, but I would like to keep this as clear as possible. I would like to go to now P724 which is a document that I think we sometimes refer to as Borovcanin's after-action report. It's a document that is signed by Borovcanin that we've received from him, and this is a document that you're familiar with, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that it's dated 5 September 1995, but that we see in the title of it under "report" that it was from the period of 11 July to 21 July. And I do not want to go through all the detail of it, but I do want to ask you about a couple of details. I mean, we can see that it starts out by providing the order 64/95 and that is the 10 July order that we just referred to earlier and begins to provide a chronology. The first thing I want to ask you about, it should be on page 2 in the English. It may be page 3 in the B/C/S, and we see at the top of the page in English he's talking about when he arrived in Bratunac on the 11th. He mentions Pribicevac and then going to Pribicevac. And he says here: "... I contacted General Mladic who personally commanded over the operation. On receipt of combat papers, he ordered me to go that same day with all available manpower and equipment from the direction of Zuti Most to Potocari and Milacevici ..." Now, we saw in the 10 July document that he was to report to Krstic, but I think you've explained that, that with Mladic present, he would have reported to Mladic. Now, the fact that Mladic issued him this order, does that clear up any issues of who's -- who he's under the command of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's evidently clear that Borovcanin believes that he's under the command of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that day, on the 11th, did he do -- did he actually -- was he able to follow those orders and attack from Zuti Most or did that happen later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he notes, he -- his units weren't fully assembled at that time, but, in fact, that course of action was taken, beginning the morning of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And going over to page 3 in the English, he's now talking about the 12th and how they did advance. He gives estimates of the people. Just the information that we're reading here on these days, does it -- is it roughly consistent with the information in your reports and in -- from the investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is. There is one or two exceptions, but I think you'll point those out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see, for example: "... we received information from state security employees that 12.000 to 15.000 able-bodied men, mostly armed Muslims, were moving from Srebrenica towards Konjevic Polje ..." Is that 12- to 15.000 men roughly consistent with the estimates that we have been getting over the years?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then he goes on to say: "I received an order from General Mladic to send half of my men and the available technical equipment to the axis so that to block the area and fight the aforementioned formation." Again, is this consistent with his troops on this day being under the command of Mladic and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we're getting a bit ahead of ourselves in the chronology here, but I just wanted to deal with that particular issue and that's already in evidence so I'll go on to the next Borovcanin-related document and that is 65 ter 20976A. This is an intercept you've spoken about many times over the years. It's between Krstic and Borovcanin from the Specials [Realtime transcript read in error "expeditiously"], according to the intercept operator. And I won't read it all out. It's from the 13th of July, and Krstic is asking him if he has any problems. And Borovcanin responds: "It's going well." And he confirms, again, to General Krstic that he does not have any problems. Can you put us in the chronology of the alleged criminal events. At 2040 hours on the 13th of July, had Borovcanin been present in and around any particular events, and I don't want us to conclude about any involvement at this point or anything.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As noted by the Petrovic video, then-Colonel Borovcanin is at the Kravica warehouse at approximately 1700 hours on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And regarding the command issue, how would this -- this conversation fit into your view? Can you glean anything from any kind of command relationship in a discussion like this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And in fact, this conversation occurs shortly after a ceremony at the Drina Corps headquarters presided by General Mladic, where General Krstic is promoted from the position of the Chief of Staff to the position of the corps commander of the Drina Corps. So now in his capacity as the corps commander, General Krstic is calling subordinates and getting reports from them as to what the current situation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would object, as we have for these intercepts, that they have not been authenticated sufficiently so as to be proven reliable. I -- looking at this one, I believe this is -- no, I'm not sure that this is an ABiH intercept to which this witness has testified about. So that would be an additional objection. I believe this was from some other entity, although I'm not sure whether we're allowed to talk about it in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, do we have to -- do we need to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have an opportunity to respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this intercept is already in evidence as P01294; however, it is the -- only the handwritten version of the intercept, and therefore the date from, as you may recall, the print-out of the intercept is not on the document that's in evidence. So I've offered the 65 ter version of it with the appropriate print-out version which gives the date and it's been blocked out in black, as was the agreed procedure so that it would not be confused with other intercepts. And we are endeavouring for these intercept issues to sort them out so that you see the intercepts and you see the dates with them. It's a rather complex issue that we're -- that I don't believe there's really any -- I don't think we're contesting -- there's any contest about that particular part of it. But that is a bit of the confusion why I offer this particular intercept into evidence, so that we're getting the print-out version, basically. The other part is really in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the substance is in evidence I do understand and -- from McCloskey and the date, it's just -- the matter apparently is how the Chamber will get acquainted with the dates rather than whether. Any further comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, we have, I think, even at the time that the other witnesses who came to testify about intercepts, always maintained our objection, and I believe -- I can't speak for this one because I believe it is a witness that I did not cross, but the issue of whether -- what date is for a particular intercept I think should have been addressed with that witness, not through this witness. So again, I believe that for purposes of -- of the intercepts, we maintain our objection from before. And I understand that Your Honours have admitted certain intercepts for varying reasons into evidence already, but I simply think that at this time through this witness if -- you know, I don't know how he can provide information that was not available when the other witnesses testified as to the handwritten versions that were -- of this one that was introduced. I don't have it in front of me now to be able to see if it's the exact same, et cetera, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think wisest thing to do would be to give you an opportunity to again revisit the details, Mr. Ivetic, and then hear your final position and we'll then decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you just explain for me why you are tendering this if it is already in evidence as P1294?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll -- it's probably best that I show you. If we could go to P01294. And, by the way, I know Mr. Butler is very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public because it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I know Mr. Butler is very familiar with this -- all this material, but this is the document that came in through the bar table in evidence. And as you can see, this is from the handwritten notebook of the 2nd Corps which, as you may recall, is the -- we had the original handwritten notes. But you also may recall that the dates were not always written in the notebook. Once they gave the notebook to the typist, they typed out on an e-mail-type arrangement and that always injected the date. And so this came in through the bar table motion in an abbreviated format with just the page of the handwritten notebook. If we go back through the notebook, you can eventually find a date and then go forward to realise the date, but there's a lot of pages and a lot of extra in that and it's really clearly established with the print-out. So we have kept these to a minimum; however, in so doing, some of the intercepts don't have the date. And so in order to avoid the problem of not having a date and the record, we have been able to come up with the date from the print-out in this case and put it in another format. The dates of the intercepts have never been contested; the intercepts themselves have. The records are very clear, and the only problem is in our efforts to make this simpler it may have become a bit more complex and we're working on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But with respect, I still don't understand why you're tendering something that is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because there's no dates on the one that's in evidence, there's no date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we see -- Mr. Ivetic, is there any chance that the parties could stipulate that the date under which this handwritten -- this handwritten excerpt of the -- of these intercepts appears is the date as we find it now, that is, the 13th of July if I'm not mistaken? I mean, I'm not talking about anything else but the date to be found in that handwritten version but not on this page. Would you consider that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would consider that, Your Honour. We, of course, maintain our position that we believe these intercepts are not generated at the time that they are dated, but I believe that we could probably agree that the text of two purported intercepts do appear to relate -- be recorded as being a particular date, although we reserve objection to that being the actual date at which time they were authored. And that would perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at least that what is written down in this transcription of the intercept is a date, 13th of July. And let's see -- because if that would be a stipulation, Mr. -- would we still need --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- that's one way to resolve it, but the -- while the handwritten materials are -- in a sense they're the inked originals, it really is quite an analysis and sometimes to going back through them to determine the date because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- as you recall the testimony, people wrote dates sometimes and sometimes they didn't. So it's quite an analysis. We've been through this in previous trials where each intercept operator has testified. That's one of the reasons why many of these were in evidence in previous cases already which is one of the justifications why you've allowed them in evidence here. The best way to get the dates is this print-out, the electronic print-out, that goes with many of them; and where we don't have print-outs for a few, then we go through this more complicated process of the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're invited to seek agreement with the Defence whether you could stipulate that the 13th of July is the date which features in the document, perhaps on previous pages, and that this therefore is covered by that date, true or not, but it's written down there. In that case, we would need the new exhibit you are suggesting. Therefore, it will be marked for identification at this moment and we'll later decide, after you've talked to the Defence, whether the number can be vacated. Mr. Registrar, the number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 65 ter number 20976A will be MFI P2105 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2103"] under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we hear from you, let's say, later this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Of course, there will be many more intercepts with a similar problem, but what Mr. Ivetic has said gives me some hope that we can agree to argue over some things but not perhaps the date. So we will get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On this -- in relation to this document, just one observation in relation to the transcript, page 40, line -- lines 3 and 4, the sentence - this is a part of the submission by Mr. McCloskey - should read "it's between Krstic and Borovcanin from the specials" and not "expeditiously," because we can take that from the translation of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, that is what I said and that's, of course, an important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we get a confirmation of the MFI number? We see 2103 on the screen, is that correct, or was it 2105?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's MFI P2105.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Stewart, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After a diversion into the special police and intercepts, let's go back to the narrative chronology and if we could go to 65 ter 4168, and as that's coming up on our screen we'll see that it's from the Main Staff, second page in the English, it's from General Mladic and it's an order to the commands of the Drina Corps and the 65th Protection Regiment. And it says: "Taking the defence line and improving the tactical position. "Order." And it's basically talking about close the Zepa enclave. Mr. Butler, briefly what is this and what does it show in your view regarding General Mladic's knowledge of the battle-field situation that we have on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly the Main Staff and in general and General Mladic in particular have been keeping aware of the successes at Srebrenica and, as they would normally be expected to do, they are already starting to anticipate what those successes mean and what steps that they should be taking in the future in order to continue to maintain the momentum. What you see in this order is essentially on the 10th anticipating continued success, he's ordering forces, some from the Drina Corps, some from the 65th Protection Regiment, to undertake or prepare to undertake operations beginning on the 12th in order to take advantage of the continuing favourable situation at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: By the 10th of July, the -- they haven't even been into Srebrenica yet. In your view, is this proper planning on the general's part? Or is he really jumping ahead of the game when he should be concentrating on the business at hand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would definitely have the opinion that he is properly doing what he is supposed to be doing. It's -- on 10 July it's General Krstic's job to fight the immediate battle at Srebrenica, and on 10 July it's General Mladic's job, as the next higher headquarters, to set the stage and circumstances for the next operation. Generals are taught as part of their professional training to not think in the present; they need to think in the future. So the fact that General Mladic is already thinking ahead for potential opportunities is exactly what he should be doing as a function of his professional training and his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the document consists of two orders. It's -- in English it's a five-page document, the first is an order and that in English takes two pages, I think in the B/C/S original only one page. And then we have a page in the original almost completely illegible apart from some text at the bottom. And then we have another order. Is it your intention to tender both orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out. It's my understanding that they're identical orders, though we have writing on the top of one and so that we gave you a translation of that second one as well. And I didn't get into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then -- because we see that on page 4 of the English, Mr. Butler, we will see that in the handwritten section of the second copy of that first order it says: "Prepare operationally our order, order sent on 11 July 1995," and it's signed by someone. And we also see the "Operations Duty Officer, Predrag Jocic." What can you tell us about that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, as was customary at the time, making sure everyone that got the order, it looks from the various -- the way that this is, that what essentially the Drina Corps did was essentially re-transmit a portion of the order to the Drina Corps headquarters as well as the IKM to personally ensure that the general saw it. Operations Duty Officer Predrag Jocic is of the Drina Corps. So this simply looks like a re-transmission, maybe a slight amplification, but making sure it's directed to the two leadership officials of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic and General Krstic, to ensure that they personally receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they're not exactly the same, but the one was immediate follow-up to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you, Mr. President, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, there were no objections. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 65 ter number 04168 will be Exhibit P2106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2106 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to 65 ter 04221.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a daily combat report from the Bratunac Brigade under the name of Commander Blagojevic. I believe you've actually made reference to something like this. I would point out -- I'm sorry the B/C/S is so difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps the second paragraph in the Serbian could be blown up, though we do have the handwritten version as well. If we flip in the B/C/S to the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you explain how for Bratunac documents -- you've actually looked at documents taken from the Bratunac Brigade. Can you explain how it is there is a written and a handwritten?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When we were processing the documents as a result of the OTP's document seizure at Bratunac in 1998, one of the things that we noted on many of the Bratunac Brigade orders was that they were initially written by hand by the officer in question. They were then taken over to the communications centre, where they were then typed on to the requisite Teletype machine and sent. And what their filing process was, was that they would actually physically staple the handwritten document to the Teletype version of the document and put it in the files there. So what you have with these Bratunac documents is you will have the handwritten document by the original author, whoever it would be on any given day, and you will also have the Teletype version of that document that was -- that was forwarded to whatever command the order or document was sent to.
