So you'll always have in many -- where you have a handwritten one and where you have a Teletype version, that explains why you have two versions of the same order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know -- if when we see a document like this, do you know whether this was handwritten by the duty officer or the -- or Blagojevic, whose name is under it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally with daily combat reports, the author of the document is the duty operations officer. That is one of his standard duties. He will write the signature block of the commander, because obviously the commander goes -- is responsible for the document and the duty operations officer on that day is the commander's authorised representative. So with documents like this, the fact that it says "Commander Colonel Blagojevic," it doesn't necessarily mean that he wrote that report and that the writing on the document will match his. It's just this report is going out in the commander's name. It is -- it is the commander's daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say he should be responsible for it. In your view of reading all these documents, were brigade commanders such as Blagojevic, Vinko Pandurevic, did they keep abreast of what was going out in their name as their daily combat reports and other documents and reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did. Obviously if you're a commander, you need to be aware of reports that are going out in your name. If you weren't the actual author of the report, what they would often do is at some point at the end of the day, when they got back to their desk or from wherever they returned from the field, there would be a series of documents that were published by the brigade, such as daily combat reports and things of that nature, so the commanders would have an opportunity to review them and know what their brigade had sent to the higher headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then just looking at this particular document, paragraph 2, it -- it's noted that: "General Mladic, Major-General Zivanovic, Major-General Krstic, and the commanders of the Corps brigades, which are participating in offensive activities, are in the area of responsibility of the 1st Bratunac Brigade." As we know the abbreviation to be. Is this what you mentioned previously when you talked about indications of the whereabouts of General Mladic on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again not only General Mladic going to the Drina Corps forward command post to observe operations, but General Zivanovic, who is still at this time the corps commander. So you have no mention now of General Gvero. The presumption is that General Gvero has now departed since General Mladic is physically present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objections to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04221 will be Exhibit P2107, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2107 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could now go to 65 ter 00380.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another document from the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, again dated 10 July in the name of -- it says actually "for the Commander Colonel Blagojevic." And we can note here that it says: "Pursuant to the order of the Commander of the Main Staff, the Army of Republika Srpska, aimed at breaking the enemy offensive in Bratunac and Srebrenica municipality areas, I hereby order ..." And then we see it's an order to mobilise, compulsory work, people and others. What does this indicate to you, aside from the substance of the order itself, does this provide to you any indication of General Mladic, where he is, what he's doing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Clearly as from -- evidenced by the prior document, General Mladic is present on the ground and at the IKM, and as this indicates, he is engaged with what is going on. At this point in time, on 10 July, as the mission has been changed now to take or liberate the town of Srebrenica, they realise they need additional manpower. And this is one of a number of orders that goes out to the brigades to be sent to the Ministry of Defence in order to mobilise additional soldiers who currently were not on active duty because they are on compulsory work obligation in the civilian economy. And I believe that you will see on the second page of this document, where they list where these companies are and how many soldiers that each of these companies is expected to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go there, the second page, both. Okay. And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 00380 will be Exhibit P2108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2108 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter 5816. And I apologise, I can see from the English translation we have missed "Glavni Stab Vojske," but we know that's the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, dated 11 July, and if we go to the second page in the English and further on in the Serbian, we'll see that it's in the name of General Mladic. And we'll also -- can we go to the Serbian. And in the Serbian we can see that General Mladic in a stamp -- we don't see a signature, but we see what I believe should be "SR" which didn't make it into the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, what is your understanding of "SR"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll send this to have it revised, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding from the practice on -- that I've seen on the military documents is that -- and again as I discussed earlier how the signature blocks of the commanding officers would be drafted by subordinates and oftentimes signed for them if they were authorised to do so. When you see the abbreviation "SR" after the signature, it's designed to let the reader know that that signature -- the signature is actually that of the commander or the authorised individual and it's not of a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the -- just the front of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What does "SR" stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just -- we see this 11 July order. Can you just briefly tell us what you recollect this order to be about? I don't want to read it all, but we can see it speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As noted in this particular order and not previously known to the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska, a number of individuals from the command of the 28th Infantry Division were actually not in the enclave at the time the operation began, specifically the commander of the 28th Division, Naser Oric, and I think upwards of 15 or 20 of his staff officials, they were actually in Tuzla and later in Sarajevo, where they were undertaking planning of future military operations against the Drina Corps. This document reflects the fact that the Army of the Main Staff from, as they say, from verified information is now warning their subordinates, the Drina Corps and other units, that they have learned that Naser Oric and other command -- members of the command of the main -- of the 28th Division were not in the enclave, and further that they had information that they may very well be setting up a military operation to try and break into the enclaves in order to relieve the 28th Infantry Division. And further, based on this information, they're ordering various units to start to prepare for that eventuality and to take precautionary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we first look at this document a bit more in detail. At the end of the English version I see that there is a box which very much looks like a -- the kind of stamp filled in which is missing in the original. So there seems to be something translated which doesn't match with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore, it seems that although the text may be the same and, to that extent, the translation may be a reliable one, that at least it's most likely taken from another version of, again, likely the same document. You see that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is the second mystery stamp that's appeared, and I appreciate you pointing that out. We'll sort this out at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, from what I see comparing the original to the extent that I can decipher some of the words, it seems that it's -- it's about the same more or less, but ... Mr. Ivetic, apart from the stamp, is there any issue about the English version to reflect the text of the original one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe, apart from the stamp and the associated text that is part of the stamp, the translation does purport to the text of the original. We do have an issue as to the authenticity of the original, given the lack of a signature and other factors. But it has not yet been tendered, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has not been tendered yet, but I would not be surprised if it would soon. Mr. McCloskey, if you sort this out, perhaps you can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I will. And of course, we know that many, many documents have no signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a different matter. But we now see an English translation with a huge stamp and a lot of text filled in as we often see it which does not appear on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, absolutely, we'll fix that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to -- so that counsel is aware of the full nature of our objection. We now know that General Mladic was not at that location the 11th of July, 1995, and so therefore we believe that he could not have issued this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "that location"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff. The originator -- what is claimed to be the origination of the document. I'm trying to open it back up on my screen to get the first page since we only have the second page in e-court. But it is said to originate from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look. That may be another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then there's also some -- the handwritten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, Mr. McCloskey, in view of the fact that apparently the translation is not reflecting exactly what there is in the original, the explanation that the "Glavni Stab Vojske" was by mistake not being translated needs further attention as well. Apparently part of the original which doesn't exist is translated and part of what is there is not translated. That really needs further attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you'll give it to it, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll sort that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed meanwhile. Should we -- perhaps we should mark it for identification but it's not tendered yet, but -- so that we at least know what the whole discussion was about the last couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Um, yeah, that's a very good idea. It's also their special number 03/4-1616. That's the ID number on the document of the VRS, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that is there in the translation, although it doesn't say "handwritten," which usually is the case. Then there is another matter that is the handwriting in the translation. On the top right corner it says "handwritten: 14878," whereas that seems not to appear in the original, where it reads: "65.2" perhaps "motorised brigade," I do not know. But certainly the translation is not in line with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will sort that out. You have now I think two or three problems to resolve in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's mark it for identification so that it's at least on the record what we were talking about. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 05816 will be MFI P2109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status. Please proceed -- no, not perhaps proceed. We should take a break. We ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is escorted into the courtroom and we'll wait for him to arrive. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, I have been tracking down original documents. We'll sort this out with the Defence, Mr. President. We do have several versions of this particular document from several locations, the three from the Drina Corps collection, one from the Banja Luka archives, which you've heard about. The one that we're using now is from the Banja Luka archives, but we have three Teletypes from the original Drina Corps collection. Various translations, none of which are perfect, so we need to get that worked out and we'll concentrate tonight and make sure that we resolve these significant issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have faith that this document is -- the substance of which is translated well, though clearly the important details are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, you've talked about the substance of this document and about the concern the VRS had the whereabouts of, you say, Naser Oric and his crew. Was there any indication that Naser Oric and his command staff did come back in strength or in any way to the Srebrenica area, as was the subject matter of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you explain this situation that we have here. We have a document that is indicated from the Main Staff and it's in the name of General Mladic with SR, and we know that for a good part, if not most of the day or all day of the day and evening, General Mladic is -- of the 11th is in the Srebrenica-Bratunac area, where we see him on video. How would it be that a document would go out like this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess, as I've testified again in the case of the previous Bratunac document, you know, the reality is that there were people at the Main Staff that were authorised to sign documents in the name of the general when the situation warranted. General Mladic might have been at the IKM and, in fact, was at the IKM on that day, but he was not out of communication with his higher headquarters and he was being briefed - as a good general he would be - on the broader situation. You will see a number of documents as we go down the line purporting to be orders or directions from the commander of the Main Staff that will go out in the name of General Miletic or General Gvero in one case. It's not remarkable. I mean, the VRS is a highly professional -- or back then was a highly professional army and had a well developed command and staff process. The officers in this process, they knew what their authorities were and I presume and may have testified in the past in various trials that they were not going to sign orders or they're not going to issue orders that they're by position not authorised to do. So when I'm looking at, you know, an order like this signed in the name of General Mladic as commander of the Main Staff, I would take that in the same way that his subordinate formations would take that order as receiving it, as an order of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before we continue, could I ask clarification on one matter. Your previous question you said to Mr. Butler that he had talked about the substance of the document and about the concern the VRS had about Naser Oric and the presence. And then -- your question was: "Was there any indication that Naser Oric and his staff did come back in strength or in any way to the Srebrenica area, as was the subject matter of this document?" Now, the answer was: "No, sir, they did not." That is not an answer to your question because you asked about the existence of any indication, so the answer could have been there was not or -- and at the same time, the document seems to express such a concern. So could I seek a clarification from the witness what he exactly wanted to tell us. Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He can go ahead and answer before we lose your point. I have another issue about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the document here reflects the VRS's understanding of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, as I know from my role in the investigation and my own research, they did not -- Naser Oric and his staff did not seek to re-enter the enclave. In fact, they were active with the 24th Infantry Division several days later trying to do that. So I guess for clarity's sake, the fact -- again, the fact that the VRS believed that they would do that is the accurate perception of the VRS at that time. As we know several days later from the historical record, Naser Oric was not seeking to get into the enclave with his command group here, but was in fact in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So "they did not" means then that they did not come back to the Srebrenica area, but at the same time you say the document shows that the VRS expected that he would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again, as you go to the first page of the document, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the verified information again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that code for they're getting this and they believe that it is reliable intelligence information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now your answer has been clarified. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I have to rise to say that this particular paragraph, this particular sentence that we've now focused on, the English translation is incorrect. It does not correlate to the B/C/S original, which I just now noticed in reading -- in hearing the question that was posed by Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that since this document needs further attention in many respects, that you inform Mr. McCloskey about your concerns about the translation and that, as part of the exercise Mr. McCloskey has to do anyhow, that he also includes a verification of the relevant portion of the document. It may be that other versions are better translated, we do not know yet, but you share that and it's hereby on the record that you challenge the translation of the specific part we looked at. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this document is MFI'd, I take it, and we'll address those concerns. Mr. Butler, you did mention Oric in Tuzla days later. Can you -- before that gets a bit hazy, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, as the historical record will note that the column's ultimate objective when it leaves Srebrenica through the route that I discussed yesterday -- I mean, they're attempting to break through at the lines of Baljkovica and Nezuk in order to reach what they call free territory, friendly territory. My understanding again from the investigation and my research on those issues are that many members of the 28th Division staff actively were working with their counterparts on the 2nd -- with the 2nd Corps, 24th Division, in order to help the 24th Division make the breakthrough in the Baljkovica and Nezuk area to allow the column to pass through. So that's what most of those individuals were actively doing on those particular days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we do know that we will get to the 16th of July, but not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 5759.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's the -- a Main Staff report to the president from all the corps. And if we could go to the Drina Corps section, which would be page 3 of both languages regarding the last part of the English --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 5797. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to page 3 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S, Drina Corps, you'll recall that these are supposed to go out in the evening. And we note that the Main Staff is telling the president: "In the Srebrenica enclave the enemy has been putting up fierce resistance to VRS units. The NATO air force carried out strikes against our forces" and it lists the sectors. "An interim report on the situation in Srebrenica and the NATO air force is forthcoming." And then it goes on to the next page in English. "The corps units are in a state of full combat-readiness. The main forces are being used to mount persistent defence, and part of the forces are involved in offensive operations around the ... enclave. In the course of the day, our forces entered the town of Srebrenica ..." It talks a bit about the NATO members, the four Dutch F-16 that took part in the Srebrenica action. Is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have the right page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it should be page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, is this information going to the president correct as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. By about 1500 on 12 July -- I'm sorry, 11 July 1995, the VRS moves into the urban environment of Srebrenica town. I take it that at some juncture, if the Court has not already seen it that they will see a rather lengthy videotape which essentially shows General Mladic as well as other VRS commanders walking through the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's get to the 12th of July, an intercept, P1212. And at 0608 hours and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and I would like to offer the last document into evidence, the Main Staff report, 5797.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2110 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, we see this intercept in the early morning hours of 12 July: "From Jaglici towards Buzim up there, towards our neighbours on the right. Let them know. They need to be warned. Do you understand? "Understood. "... a column." What is your view of what this is about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, there is a bit of a story behind this and why this particular intercept becomes significant. As indicated in other documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. It should not be broadcast, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As other individuals have provided information and, in fact, as some of the documents that we've looked at before foreshadow, the Army of the Republika Srpska forces in Srebrenica had anticipated that in the event of attack and in the event that they were successful in their operations against the 28th Infantry Division, that they would withdraw towards the Zepa enclave. Again, as the historical record notes, they did not do that. In fact, they came to an entirely different decision on what they would do, that being to form a column and that to breakout from Jaglici through the long -- smuggling -- the long-used smuggling routes through the Zvornik area and out towards Baljkovica. General Mladic, not knowing that obviously at this time and the army staff had already started on the evening of 11 July to put in place their combat preparations to send military forces towards an area known as the Bandera Triangle towards the Zepa area on the morning of the 12th. They had lost complete contact with the 28th Infantry Division and they did not know where it was. They anticipated that they would again regain contact with it in the Bandera-Suceska area and, in fact, it wasn't there. What this particular intercept is and why it suddenly becomes relevant is this is one of the first indications by people on the other side of the enclave, the correspondents who are talking here from the north -- the northern side of the enclave, that they are starting to see Bosnian Muslim military forces arrayed in a column in a location that they were not told to expect to anticipate those forces. So what you have happening through the evening of the 11th and later on through the morning hours and even early afternoon hours of the 12th is a growing realisation, as it percolates -- this information percolates up to the general officers, that the forces of the 28th Division are not where they're expected to be but are, in fact, perhaps 12 to 15 kilometres away. And by time they're learning of this information, many of the initial lead elements of the column of the 28th Division have already succeeded in breaking out over the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba and are already entering the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. So this sets in chain -- this sets in -- this sets the beginning of a chain of events into place, where you start to have two competing situations occurring with respect to Srebrenica and, of course, I'll get into them in more detail as we go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on this particular point, you've also addressed that in your narratives as well if we don't deal with some of the other things today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1217.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should consider if that could be broadcast or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I do not see any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: E-court's got it as confidential. Let's leave it that way for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We now see this as an intercept on 12 July. It's a little bit later, 0735, between Krstic and Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. And it's talking about buses and various towns and the Bratunac stadium. What is this about briefly, Mr. Butler? Just -- who are these people, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correspondent called Krstic is General Krstic, the -- still at this point Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic is the chief of transportation services for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what are they talking about, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the late evening hours and the early morning hours of 12 July, a decision is made that it won't be UNPROFOR providing vehicles, it will be the Republika Srpska that will provide all of these vehicles to remove the population that is assembled at Potocari. What you see is a series of both published orders from the army to the Ministry of Defence requesting the requisition of civilian buses. You see orders from army headquarters to other army units, telling them to send buses and trucks to Potocari and Bratunac, and you see a series of intercepts, where you have individuals who would normally be expected to be dealing with these matters on the telephones, ensuring that orders are complied with and that buses and trucks are sent to locations as rapidly as possible. One of the reasons why I use -- believe -- and believe this is significant is that this is something that obviously was not planned for in advance of the operation. Had it been done so, the ability to assemble the buses and trucks and everything else would have been done days in advance. It would not have been done on such a rapid and haphazard way on the morning of 12 July 1995. I mean, it was an amazing logistical feat that they were to assemble them when they needed to, but it wasn't the preferred way that they would have done it had they been given a choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go over some of, perhaps, the documents you've mentioned. Let's go to P1710. This is a document from the VRS Main Staff, sector for mobilisation and personnel and it's to the RS Ministry of Defence and it's talking about making buses available and that 50 buses need to be mobilised to the Bratunac sports stadium. It's under the name of Assistant Commander Major-General Petar Skrbic. And, Mr. Butler, he has testified about this, the Judges have heard about it, so I don't think we need to spend so much time on it, but was this one of the documents that you were talking about regarding this getting together buses to remove the population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next one, P1714. This is, again, from the command of the Drina Corps, 12 July. This is -- has a stamp on it of 10 hours and 1020 hours. It's to the Main Staff, among others, and it's from General Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps. And it says: "Pursuant to the VRS GS Commander's order to provide 50 buses for evacuation from the Srebrenica ..." and it goes on. And what does this indicate to you about General Mladic's involvement in this business of buses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as evidenced by General Zivanovic, he's noting that the order to -- for these units to send buses is coming from commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document, P1509. This is also in evidence. I think it made a very brief appearance, so I'm -- our recollections may not be as refreshed as others. But we see this is from the Zvornik public security centre dated 12 July in the name of Dragomir Vasic, the chief of the public security centre. So who is he? What's this about? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Vasic is the head of the sector for security and public safety for the Zvornik region, which includes the Bratunac and now Srebrenica municipalities. So he is essentially the chief of police for about a five-municipality area that makes up the Zvornik sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see this -- this report to the police force staff and the office of the minister and others. It mentions Miroslav Deronjic, but on paragraph 2: "A meeting with General Mladic and General Krstic was held at the Bratunac Brigade command at 0800 hours, at which tasks were assigned to all participants." What, if anything, does this tell you about General Mladic's command and who he is commanding at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates, again, General Mladic is actively taking charge of events and his physical presence there. He is in command and he is acting as he is in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see in 3: "The military operation is continuing according to plan. The Turks are fleeing towards Suceska, while the civilians have gathered in Potocari ..." This reference to the Muslims fleeing towards Suceska, can you remind us where Suceska is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suceska is a region on the southern end of the enclave. Again, as indicated in my earlier testimony on this, in fact, their information is not correct or accurate to their knowledge yet and the column is on the north end of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it also talks about that: "A meeting will begin at 1000 hours ..." And in your view was that the meeting that has been seen on video that the Court has previously seen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in number 6: "Joint police forces are advancing on Potocari with the aim of taking UNPROFOR ..." Is that related to Borovcanin's forces and the order he had received from Mladic that you had mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document, and this is a document we will get a better copy of because in your understanding, Mr. Butler, who is this document from, though I'm -- it says "chief of the CJB," but it's not legible.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document I believe is from Mr. Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasic, I'm sorry, not Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's another Mr. Vlasic. All right. Let's -- and we can see from this document, this is basically the same report a bit later in the day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see it says: "At 1030 hours a meeting was held at the hotel in Bratunac attended by the following" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have it on our screens already?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe he gave the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 5818. Thank you. I will slow down. And I will note that the previous document 1509 had an internal Zvornik CJB number of 277. We can see that this one is number 278.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it notes: "At 1030 hours a meeting was held at the hotel in Bratunac attended by ..." We can see that General Mladic is there, Vasic is there, Miroslav Deronjic, Karremans, the Muslim representatives. Does this reflect a reference to the meeting of -- that part of what is on the video that's part of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is what we call the third meeting at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you can see the information that they have there. I just wanted to ask you about number 4: "It was decided to grant their requests and with UNPROFOR assistance (presence and provision of fuel for transportation) and the trucks were provided, boarding of the vehicles will commence at 1400 hours and escort will be provided till Kladanj ..." And as far as you know, did that basically happen on that time-frame?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think the first convoys went out probably a little earlier, maybe around noon, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it says: "After the inspection, depending on Mladic's decision, able-bodied men may be allowed to go in order to have the others from the woods to surrender, since our command urged them to do so." Can you tell us what you take this to mean and what you take it to -- how you fit it into your analysis regarding Vasic's knowledge of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the key observations and, in fact, opinions that I have historically made with respect to when an order was made to kill the prisoners is that that order must have been given between the end of the second meeting at the Hotel Fontana at 2200 hours on 11 July and before the third meeting at the Hotel Fontana the next morning at 1000 hours, based on my own constructive analysis of when other events started occurring on the battle-field and along the broader crime base. One of the issues that, of course, we have dealt with in previous proceedings against other defendants is at what point news of the order that has been issued reaches them, and you can see at various points in time various officials who need to know of the order learn of it and that people who don't need to know of the order don't learn of it until later when they hear of it. In this particular context, you know, Dragomir Vasic as the head of CSB Zvornik is reporting in his document as though the able-bodied men, you know, may be set or may be let free. It indicates that he has not been read into the plan, which is actually that the able-bodied men will be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we will go through the documents and the factors and, of course, that ultimate determination of an order will be one for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 05818 will be Exhibit P2111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2111 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now P1232.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept from 12 July. It's a MUP -- confidential, please. A MUP intercept. We can see that it's at 1220 hours and it's between two unidentified people, X and Y. It's a mention of Miletic and they're speaking about fuel and trucks leaving from various places. And it makes a reference about 2 tonnes in Zvornik, there is nine, there is no more. Can you tell us what you take this to mean and who you believe Miletic would be in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miletic in this context is General Miletic, the chief of operations for the Main Staff. The issue that they're talking about is that with 50 and -- and as it turns out, even more than that buses and trucks descending on Potocari and there were requirements to shuttle people from Potocari, from there, to Kladanj, come back. The issue, of course, at hand is that they're scrambling now to try and get enough fuel for all of these buses and trucks to be able to remove the population from Potocari as quickly as possible under the circumstances. There are a number of intercepts where you see the issue of: Where is the fuel coming from and how fast can we get it here? As a matter of importance to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Miletic is not an uncommon name. Why would a general in the Main Staff be dealing with fuel issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, the Republika Srpska was suffering from a number of embargoes, one of them was fuel in an effort to pressure them as well as all of the parties to end the conflict. To us, 10.000 gallons of diesel fuel does not sound like a large amount of fuel; but in the context of the fuel shortage that is occurring, as well as the broader needs of the army for fuel on any given day, 10.000 gallons of diesel fuel or 10.000 litres of diesel fuel even, here it's tonnes, this is a big deal to the army. They have to be able to get this fuel, it has to be brought in from some places. And the local units do not have anywhere near the required amount of diesel fuel to make this happen. So it takes the order of the Main Staff to the large logistics depots, who will have this fuel, in order to have that fuel transferred down to the other units for their use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are there other intercepts and/or indications that General Miletic is involved in this, some of which you may note in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. General Miletic as the chief of operations is involved in many of these aspects. He's involved in the fuel aspect and in the coming days in terms of intercepts, you can also find intercepts where he's monitoring the activities of the column and the military situation as it's occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another intercept, P01233. And if you could look at this as it comes up - confidential, please - as this is a Bosnian -- this is a 2nd Corps intercept, where we have the print-out associated with it. At 1240 hours. And have you studied this intercept, do you know what date this intercept is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see it says: "We are starting the evacuation of those who want to go towards Kladanj." Can you tell us, though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one thing. You said it's the 12th of July. Now, we earlier had a discussion about dates of intercepts. What's the basis for your knowledge that it's the 12th of July? Is that because you saw previous portions of the same [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, again, I've been working with these intercepts since 1998/1999, and as part of the corroboration of them and date-timing of them, I've worked with these things before. I have these documented in my report, what day and what time I believe that they are based on that larger corroboration effort. I know this to be 12 July, put it in my report as such. I'm sure that it's because that I also went back and did the corresponding look at the 2 Corps what we call the larger dot matrix document, the typed document, as well as I've been back and gone through the books as well when I felt I needed to go back and corroborate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see at the top "inaudible" in parenthesis and then "Panorama" and X and then Y and "barely audible." Can you tell us had your investigation, your analysis revealed the identity of -- or what is this Panorama?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As part of the communication protocols that the VRS used, various headquarters and various units were provided with a telephonic identity. So you would potentially get on a telephone and be able to identify what unit you are versus a code word that the other correspondent would recognise, but if the communication was intercepted, they wouldn't know who it was presumably. The problem was that these guys never changed their telephonic code words. So it never changed and ultimately anyone can figure out who it was. In this particular context, "Panorama" was the telephonic code name for the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, "never" is a pretty big word. Can you narrow that down for us? Do you know what time-periods were between changing or do you stand by "never"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly within the context of the intercepts that I've worked with, June, July, August, September of 1995, these telephonic code words did not change, they remained the same with respect to this particular communications network. So during the period that I discussed this in my report, "Panorama" is always the telephonic code-name for the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute as to "Panorama" standing for the Main Staff of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've heard this evidence before, Mr. McCloskey. It's not disputed, so why spend further time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the first I've learned that it's not disputed, so I'm very happy about that and I won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was at least not challenged, I think, during the cross-examination of the witness who testified about it. So therefore that's not exactly the same but that's what made me ask the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, thank you. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while we're on that topic, can you tell us the code-name for this time period for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Zlatar, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any dispute about that, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No dispute about Zlatar being the code-name for the Drina Corps? May I take it Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As to July of 1995, there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Palma, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Badem, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in looking at this, we see that the barely audible, unknown Y is saying: "And reinforce ... with trucks and buses, and a water tank should be sent, to give them water and food. This morning we organised it here, we'll give them everything. I talked with them and we'll accept all the civilians who want to and they can stay. Those who don't want to can choose where they'll go." Where do you think this information -- who -- would be coming from and what have you made of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in this particular case, this is an example of one of those intercepts that I spoke about yesterday, where the authenticity of the intercept I believe is without question; however, it is clear that at least the correspondent Y talking on the intercept does not have factually accurate information of the decision that has been made. He does not know that at this point other orders have been given that everyone will be going and that no one will be given a choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you have any backup to that statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there are other intercepts as well as other evidence that it's been led - and I don't know it off the top of my head at the moment - which reflects that despite public statements by the VRS, that the reality was that the order had been given that everyone was going to be removed from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the witness know what evidence is led in this case? Because that's what he suggests and, to some extent, refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not followed the proceedings of this case, so I am at somewhat of a disadvantage knowing what the Trial Chamber has or has not heard yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not at a disadvantage. You just should answer the questions and then not bother about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what other evidence we've heard. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1235. This is also confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a CSB state security Muslim intercept and this is at 1250 hours, ten minutes after the last one. And it's a conversation identified by the intercept person as General Mladic and an unidentified male, X. And we can see the first few lines about the buses -- have the buses and trucks left is a question Mladic asks. X says: "They have?" Mladic says: "When?" X says: "Ten minutes ago?" Mladic says: "Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to." X says: "I understand, General." He goes on to say: "Don't issue any statements and don't interrupt them over the" something "station. We'll open a corridor towards Kladanj." X can't be heard. Mladic says: "Indeed, let it pass there. Take a patrol of ours and wait on the road and remove the mines and obstacles ... leave the territory." X says: "Yes, General." What do you think General Mladic is referring to when he says "and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to" -- I should say preceded by "they've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the individuals who are at this point in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For your analysis, does that clear up any issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in context with the other events that are occurring, it supports my position that regardless of what some of the public statements were, that the intention of General Mladic at this juncture was that everyone would be removed from Potocari, that there was not a realistic choice that people could stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by the end of 13 -- end of the day 13 July, did your investigation reveal that any significant numbers of Muslim civilians left in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of 13 July 1995, the VRS themselves are reporting -- several officers from the VRS Main Staff who are on the ground in Bratunac and Potocari are reporting back through their chain of command that everyone is gone and that there are not Bosnian Muslims remaining there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask. "Don't let small groups of them sneak in." Sneak in where in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I try to stay away from putting too much of an interpretation into that. I know what happened -- what's happening at Potocari at this time, where the able-bodied men are being separated from the women and children, but I wouldn't feel comfortable trying to impart that General Mladic might be talking about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that you -- and you have no idea what -- what else could have been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of any alternative explanations which would explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time you don't feel confident to link it to that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My general rule when interpreting the intercepts and when looking at documents is to try and be as conservative with them as possible, precisely because I don't -- again, where many of the documents can be self-evident once you understand the military context that's occurring, I feel somewhat uncomfortable trying to impart what somebody really might mean and might mean down the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, we are either now or it's in five minutes from now that we have used one full hour, but if you consider this to be a more suitable moment, we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we started at 20 minutes past 12.00 -- well, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One answer to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a few minutes after 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ah. I remember -- it must have been Ms. Stewart that was late. I'm sorry. I'm sorry, that was a poor attempt at humour. There's one other slight subject matter of this intercept which we could clear up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you -- do you know what he's talking about when he says: "We'll open a corridor towards Kladanj"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he goes on to say: "... remove mines and obstacles ..."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The route that they intended to remove the population ultimately goes -- is the road network that runs from Vlasenica to Kladanj, that area is controlled by the Vlasenica Infantry Brigade and there will be a subsequent intercept where I believe it is General Mladic is calling the Vlasenica Brigade and instructing them to remove the obstacles and that they should expect the first convoys in buses and trucks to be arriving and giving them instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's go to P1236, probably keep it confidential, not shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, you'll see that this is another intercept from a notebook at 1305 hours between Krstic and Sobot and it says: "Krsmanovic set off towards Krstic 15 minutes ago?" We don't have a date on the notebook page here. Have you from your analysis determined what date that this occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I -- is it the same explanation as the last -- the last intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this the intercept you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a conversation between General Krstic and Major -- or he's looking for Major Kosoric, the commander of the Vlasenica Brigade, and in fact ends up talking with Savo, who is, I believe, Savo Sarkic who was the Chief of Staff of the Vlasenica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what are they talking about, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're talking about the route that the buses will take and General Krstic is giving instructions about where people will be disembarking, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the tunnel, where do you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the tunnel that at the time separated the territory under the control of the Republika Srpska versus the ABiH along the road from Vlasenica to Kladanj, so that's -- that tunnel is where the lines were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when Krstic near the bottom says: "Take care, nothing must happen to any of them." Who's he referring to, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take that that he's referring to the people on the buses and trucks, that they're -- when they disembark at the Tisca area, nothing is to happen to them, allow them to walk through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document -- actually, I think I'll skip one and go to 65 ter 4134. And this is from the command of the Drina Corps intelligence department dated 12 July 1995, very urgent, to the Main Staff, intelligence affairs sector, intelligence administration, Bratunac IKM, personally to Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. And it's from Major Pavle Golic. Can you tell us who Golic and Kosoric are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric is the chief of intelligence for the Drina Corps. Major Pavle Golic is his intelligence assistant, also of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see the subject matter of this shows that Golic is reporting that: "Large enemy group which included soldiers, women and children, about a thousand strong, was moving from the direction of Srebrenica between Ravni Buljim ... and was somewhere around Boksin Potok." Does this fit in to what you told us earlier about the direction of the column of people that are moving at the time and the knowledge of the VRS as they're becoming aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we also see as we go down the page a reference to the duty officer of the Drina Corps, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic, and the operations officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic. Now we'll recall that this 1994 document from the Bratunac Brigade commander was a Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic. Is this the same person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is. At this point in time he's now an operations officer with the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04134 will be Exhibit P2112, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2112 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 4223.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a -- from the command of the Bratunac Brigade, it's a daily combat report under the name of Commander Blagojevic. We see a -- a time at the bottom of it, 1630. And number 1 we see what it says in the direction of the enemy break through in the direction of Jaglici-Bokcin Potok. Is that the direction you were talking about? So at this time what does this tell us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, by the late afternoon of 12 July 1995 at least the command entities of the VRS and the Drina Corps and the subordinate brigades have all finally accepted the idea that there is a large, as yet to be undefined, number in that column of Bosnian Muslims who are trying to break out of the former enclave along this particular route. What you see as part of this particular aspect is that while now all of the various commanders understand that there is a column breaking out, there is a major disconnect, so to speak, between the assessments of the local commanders on the ground who are providing extremely large numbers for the column and the danger that it poses to the Zvornik area versus the senior leaders of the Drina Corps and of the Main Staff who believe that the number is far lower and the threat is correspondently much less. And there are a series of documents and intercepts where you essentially have local commanders requesting desperately for help and assistance because of the pending military threat, and frankly their superiors believing they are overreacting to this threat because the information they have is that it can't be this big, the numbers that they're receiving are a lot lower. So there is a corresponding period where the people most threatened actually have the best picture of what's going on and their commanders are continuing to underestimate the threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when this -- I'll jump ahead of time a bit on that point. When this large column hit the rear of the 2nd Battalion up at Baljkovica and the forces of Vinko Pandurevic, how many casualties -- how many Serb soldiers died in that -- in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the total numbers that were explained by Pandurevic - and they're listed in his 18 July interim combat report - I think he says something along the lines of between 20 -- approximately -- if I remember correctly, and I know we have the document in here down the line, 20 dead and maybe up to 80 injured. That does not include other casualties that were taken by other elements. It was particularly fierce fighting for that several-day period, some of the most fierce fighting of the war I suspect in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And number 7 in this document: "The transport of the Turkish population (Muslim refugees from the village of Potocari towards Kladanj) is in progress. A large number (10.000) of refugees are expecting to be transported from Potocari to Kladanj." Does that reflect what the investigation revealed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The convoys coming out of Potocari continued until about sundown on 12 July 1995 because once the sun went down, the road network between Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, and Nova Kasaba was no longer secure because of course the column -- the rear elements of the column kept trying to push across the road over the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I offer that document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04223 will be Exhibit P2113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2113 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P1510.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document from Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic from the Drina Corps IKM at Bratunac dated the 12th of July at 1730 hours to the Main Staff, sector for intelligence and security affairs, command of the Drina Corps and the security department. And: "In the course of the day our forces and MUP forces did not have any heavy exchange of fire with balijas. MUP forces entered Potocari in the morning without combat." It goes on to describe the remaining groups are going towards Suceska and Ravni Buljim and contact with some of the enemy. This is one of the many times we have seen in some official documents senior officers referring to the enemy. Here Pandurevic -- excuse me, Popovic is referring to the Muslims as balijas. We just saw Blagojevic's report going out under the Turkish population. And we've seen General Tolimir, General Mladic, and others referring to the term -- these sorts of terms. What is your view -- what kind of -- what does this mean -- what kind of message, if any, does this send to the -- to troops in a military?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object to the witness being asked to explain what it means. He has not been qualified for that. I don't believe that he's identified that he's fluent in the language or that he has performed any studies in literary -- not literary but I'm losing the word. In a sense of -- a lingual sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And my question was not meant in a lingual sense. We're taking the CLSS and his knowledge that "balijas" is a derogatory term for Muslims. I don't think that's -- that's common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object. The CLSS translations, in fact, is an OTP translation, a draft translation, and I was going to object to that very same fact that it's testifying not translating the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the position of the Defence that "balijas" is not a derogatory term for Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have had evidence at this trial, Your Honours, that the warring parties called each other by different names. That the Muslims called the fighters on the other side "Chetniks" and that the Serbs called the fighters on the other sides Muslims -- "balijas," sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's limited for fighters?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it derogatory?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the sense you're talking about an enemy I mean -- you're asking me to testify, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking what the position of the Defence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The position of the Defence is that this document translated by the Prosecution is offering evidence rather than translating the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking your position on a question I did put to you not to evade that question. My question was whether balijas -- whether that's the position of the Defence that it is a reference to fighter of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether it is derogatory --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Being from Bosnia, maybe I could assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- well, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Balija" is term, if you want a linguistical explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I don't want that. I want the position of the Defence on whether "balijas" is a derogatory expression, yes or no, what your position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What if we don't have a position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have -- then say: We take no position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We take no position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can lay a little better foundation if we need to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you put another question to the witness, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, as a military professional, have you become familiar in both -- both in the United States military and other militaries that soldiers and officers will refer to their enemy in derogatory terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am familiar with that phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I won't go through the terms that are common parlance now from World War II and from every war since that we know of. Have you learned the various derogatory -- of any various derogatory terms that the opposing sides use towards each other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular conflict, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard the term "poturice"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that a derogatory term?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it to be a -- it's considered to be a derogatory term against Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you heard the phrase "fuck your balija mothers"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as to the question of whether it's a derogatory term based upon what? This witness has not been qualified as a linguist or a historical expert to know about the terminology in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he was asked about how he experienced that term to be used in the region, linguistically right or wrong is not the issue, I think, which is part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, line 10 says: Is that a derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it to be understood linguistically. I think Mr. McCloskey asked for the experience of the witness in conflicts, including this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your experience, do you see that term, "poturice," used in a derogatory fashion by the Serb forces against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is often used in their military correspondence. It's included in orders, it's included in reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is the -- is that also true of "Turks" and the term "balijas"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you heard many references in documents where Serb forces are referring to Muslims in the context of "fuck your balija mothers"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less so in documents. Certainly in intercepts that phrase we'll come across on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I meant not in -- not in documents, but in other further sources. All right. So then I would get back to my question. Having learned that, what is your view of the use of such terms in official military documents, as we have seen them, by senior officers, such as Popovic, Mladic, and Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly from the context of professional militaries, that type of language is frowned upon, particularly in official correspondence reports and documents, from senior leaders. It is a well-accepted military fact of leadership that subordinate officers and subordinate soldiers rely on their leaders and use them as role models. The fact that senior officers would throw around these derogatory terms, in effect, opens the door for junior officers and soldiers to come to believe that their use of the same language will be condoned or at least tolerated. So it is a significant military leadership and professionalism issue when you're looking at official documents and official correspondence, where you see the individuals or individual ethnic groups that are described in derogatory manners like this. It is ultimately part of a larger dehumanisation process, which is why, at least within the context of the United States military, we frown upon that and certainly while it happens it is not considered to be business as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page, page 2. We again see here that: "UNPROFOR: "Did not offer resistance and did not fire at our forces ..." It also notes that: "UNPROFOR soldiers are assisting in loading women and children into the vehicles." What I want to ask you about, we also see some of the other numbers, does -- this information that is being noted here, is that accurate as far as you know, roughly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers generally correspond to the numbers that -- again, as I've testified before, we never see an exact number of people who were in Potocari, but these numbers correspond to the known ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this last sentence or second to the last: "We are separating men from 17 - 60 years of age and we are not transporting them. We have about 70 of them so far and the security organs and the state security are working with them." Does this statement correspond to any -- any reported statement of General Mladic on that day that was part of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you will recall, several hours prior to this in time, General Mladic was noted in an intercept -- or not -- if I will recall the intercept correctly, it was noted by at least one correspondent that there is going to be a separation or a separation is occurring. So this does, in fact, correspond to what is happening, which is at that point in time men known to be or suspected to be of military age are not being allowed to board the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when it says that the so far -- the security organs and the state security are working with them, what do you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at face value, "working with them," I would suspect that at that juncture individuals are at least being questioned. I know that there has been reports related to members of the RDB who are present and they're trying to interview individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall any documents that review -- that you have reviewed related to the Bratunac MPs interviewing people, including a person named Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There is -- as part of the collection of material that was seized in Bratunac in the security office, there was handwritten notations or handwritten documents, actually, which correspond to interviews of individuals who were captured and interviewed by members of the Bratunac Brigade for intelligence value on either 12 or 13 July 1995. One of those individuals who was interviewed and provided not a statement but obviously did provide information that was written down was Mr. Resid Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your time, were any of those individuals -- were their names put through the ICRC missing list, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that Resid Sinanovic -- and I believe that all of these individuals were put against the ICRC missing list. They are -- or at the time my report was written, they were listed as missing. And I have all of this documented in a specific component of my military narrative, which lays this -- this whole set of circumstances out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document, 65 ter 4224. This is from the command of the Bratunac Brigade, 12 July, to the Drina Corps, attention Major Golic, who -- you've told us about him. And it's from Captain Pecanac. And it just provides information about the Muslims. Where does that -- can you tell from this, is Captain Pecanac involved in receiving intel in the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he is. I mean, he is a Main Staff intelligence officer or operative, as the case may be.
